newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek parliament adopts Schengen despite protests.
newsitem.headline: Greek parliament adopts Schengen despite protests.

text.p: The Greek parliament adopted the European Union's Schengen open-border pact on Wednesday despite a rebellion by opposition deputies and an all-night vigil outside by protesters including many priests and nuns.
The 300-seat house voted 142-80 -- 78 deputies were absent - for the pact, which already has seven full members including France and Germany.

Schengen, which provides for border controls between EU member states to be removed and for increased cooperation on police matters, was backed by the ruling socialist party and the main opposition conservatives.
However, 53 conservative deputies ignored their party line and voted against, while outside the parliament building some 1,000 demonstrators held a rally.
The protesters, mostly members of religious groups, spent the night outside parliament in Athens holding wooden crosses and icons and yelling religious slogans.
Thousands of police were stationed around parliament and many central streets were cut off, causing traffic chaos.
At one point, two police officers threw away their caps and joined the protesters. They were later detained.
"Today parliament adopted a shameful pact," Sister Maria, an Orthodox nun, said. "Schengen means no borders, no religion, no privacy."

The religious groups say open frontiers would threaten Greece's Christian Orthodox character. They also say identity cards to be issued to EU citizens as provided by the pact carry the number 666 in their bar code, the sign of Satan.
The protesters say the pact will turn Europe into a giant police state with citizens' personal data available to authorities through a computer network.
A number of countries, including Greece, have passed laws governing limits on the type of information the state can hold on citizens, but debate continues on whether Schengen threatens privacy.
"The Schengen agreement will go into effect when the necessary preconditions securing the privacy of Greek citizens are satisfied," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters on Tuesday.

France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain, Portugal and Germany are all full Schengen members. Greece, Austria, Italy, Denmark, Finland and Sweden have signed but not yet fully implemented the pact.
